prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision in time measurement

statement.case_for: I opened with the CMB anisotropy mapping (B050) on the strength of its scientific meaning, but after reading the full set of ballots I move the optical lattice clock to the front of my preferred configuration. It is the only candidate that eight of eight members ranked and that six placed in their top three, and, more importantly, the arguments behind that support are independent of one another and robust: Katori's magic-wavelength idea is a clear, original invention; Ye's group drove it to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18; several independent laboratories (RIKEN, JILA, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) reproduce and compare the clocks; and the results are already used to probe gravitational redshift at millimetre scales and constancy of fundamental constants. That is exactly the kind of clue from nature, delivered by an instrument, that I care about. Attribution is also the cleanest on the table: every member who ranked it proposed the same two names, and a two-person prize is natural. The pending redefinition of the second makes the timing right rather than premature.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision metrology is a less obviously surprising discovery than a new phase of matter or a new window on the universe, and the neighbouring prizes (frequency combs 2005, ion control 2012) mean the committee must be able to explain what is genuinely new about the lattice clock. A prize that is only about better numbers on a clock risks being seen as incremental. Moreover, my own first choice, the CMB mapping, speaks far more directly to our place in the universe and remains unrecognised in its WMAP/Planck form, although its attribution problem (WMAP versus Planck, large collaborations, a cap of three) is real and, as Pearce points out, the field has already been honoured in 2006 and 2019.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first as a textbook case of a technique that moved the limit of what can be measured, and sees no overlap problem with the 2005 comb prize.
responses.response: I agree on the central point and it is what moves me to put B009 first. Where I would qualify is the claim of no overlap: the lattice clock stands on the comb for its frequency readout, and a citation must therefore say plainly that the new element is the magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms in a Lamb-Dicke regime, not clock accuracy in general. If we word the citation around the invention rather than the number 1e-18, the overlap objection is answered.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B009 first as a genuine invention that lets people see things they could not before, such as gravitational redshift over millimetres, while accepting the two-person framing despite many other contributors; she would also limit EHT credit to two names.
responses.response: Her argument is persuasive: the ability to observe a relativistic effect on a laboratory table is a vivid result, and it is the sort of clue in nature I look for. I share her concern about the unlisted contributors (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates), but I do not think that blocks a Katori and Ye prize, since Katori holds the idea and Ye the performance and many-body understanding. On the EHT I take her point that a three-person credit for a collaboration of hundreds is fragile, and that she sees it more as demonstration than surprise; I still rank it above the other astrophysics items, but it is no longer my main alternative.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as an instrument-driven opening of a new window, and puts the CMB mapping fourth because 2006 and 2019 prizes may have saturated the field.
responses.response: I take the saturation argument seriously for CMB but do not think it is decisive: COBE established the blackbody and first anisotropies, Peebles was honoured for theory, whereas the precision parameter measurement that turned cosmology quantitative is a distinct discovery. Our real obstacle is attribution, and there I concede. On IceCube I disagree gently: the diffuse flux is well established, but source identification is still maturing (NGC 1068, TXS 0506+056, Galactic plane), and with Karle, Spiering and Halzen leaving out so many AMANDA, Baikal and ANTARES pioneers I place it below the clock. I would revisit it in a later year, and I would like to hear whether you believe the collaboration credit can be defended.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first as a rare case of a predicted state being realised, but concedes that BHZ credit (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) falls outside the supplied names and that the 2016 prize leaves only partial room.
responses.response: I agree that prediction followed by confirmation is attractive, but I think the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit is not a small matter: the HgTe experiment was motivated directly by their proposal, so a prize to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp would skip the step that made the experiment aim at HgTe. Together with the 2016 overlap and only three members ranking it (Mehlig placing it eighth) I cannot support it as a first choice, although I would listen if you can show that Kane and Mele's Z2 formulation alone is the decisive conceptual advance.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as a foundational quantum optics result that became the platform for superconducting quantum information, and notes the 2025 prize makes it adjacent but distinct.
responses.response: I ranked B008 fourth and I respect the scientific case, but I worry about timing and credit: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is very recent, and Wallraff, who did the first strong-coupling experiment, is not in the credited set, as you yourself note. A Schoelkopf, Girvin and Blais prize would therefore leave out an experimental protagonist. I would keep B008 as an alternative for a later year, but I do not think we should rush it into this year's configuration over a cleanly attributed clock prize.

uncertainties: Whether the citation can be worded so that the magic-wavelength lattice invention is clearly distinct from the 2005 frequency comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.

Whether a single-achievement prize to two people is preferable to pairing the clock with a second distinct achievement; the credited names for CMB (four) and the three-person cap make a combination with B050 impossible, and I have not found a second part that is clearly stronger than leaving this prize focused.
For B050, whether WMAP alone or WMAP plus Planck should be honoured and how to treat Puget; I rely on general knowledge of the roles and have not verified them independently.

I have no independent expert report in hand, so as Secretary I would still request outside evaluations on the lattice-clock lineage (Lemonde, Ludlow, Oates and others) before this configuration is final.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I did my PhD at Princeton under David Gross and co-author mainly with Thomas Van Riet; none of the shortlisted candidates is a documented collaborator, supervisor or institutional colleague, although I flag my Princeton background in case the committee wishes to consider it for B050.
